[p.54] Cloud Microservices and Rate Limiting Cloud microservices have become very popular. Rate limiting is often done through a component called the API gateway. The API gateway is a fully managed service. It handles several tasks, including rate limiting, SSL termination, authentication, IP whitelisting, and serving static content. For now, remember that the API gateway is middleware that supports rate limiting. Where to Implement Rate Limiting When designing a rate limiter, a key question is: where should we implement it? Should it be on the server-side or in the gateway? There isn't a one-size-fits-all answer. It depends on your company's technology stack, engineering resources, and goals. Evaluate your current technology stack. This includes your programming language and cache service. Make sure your programming language can efficiently handle rate limiting on the server-side. Identify the rate limiting algorithm that meets your business needs. If you do everything on the server-side, you have full control of the algorithm. You might have fewer choices if you use a third-party gateway. If you've already used a microservice architecture and have an API gateway for tasks like authentication and IP whitelisting, you can add a rate limiter to the API gateway. Building your own rate limiting service takes time. If you don't have enough engineering resources for this, using a commercial API gateway is a better choice. Algorithms for Rate Limiting Rate limiting can be done using different algorithms. Each has its own advantages and disadvantages. Although this chapter doesn't focus on algorithms, understanding them at a high level helps you choose the right one for your situation. Token bucket Leaking bucket Fixed window counter Sliding window log Sliding window counter

[p.55] Token Bucket Algorithm Overview The token bucket algorithm is a method used by internet companies, like Amazon and Stripe, to control their API requests. Here's how the token bucket algorithm works: A token bucket is like a container with a set size. Tokens are added to the bucket at regular intervals. Once the bucket reaches its limit, no more tokens can be added. For example, if the bucket can hold 4 tokens and tokens are added at a rate of 2 every second, any extra tokens beyond the capacity will spill out. When a request is made, it needs one token to proceed. First, we check if there are enough tokens available. If there are enough tokens, we take one token out for the request, and the request is approved. If there are not enough tokens, the request is rejected.

[p.56] Token Consumption and Rate Limiting Figure 4-6 shows how token consumption, refill, and rate limiting work together. This process helps control how often a resource can be used. In this example, the token bucket size is 4. This means it can hold up to 4 tokens. The refill rate is 4 tokens every 1 minute. This means that once a minute, the bucket can fill up to its full capacity of 4 tokens again.
